prompt: A server crashes halfway through its durably reserved ID range. Which recovery preserves uniqueness?

options.text: Reassign the entire range because the server is no longer running.
options.explanation: Its earlier IDs may already exist, and a delayed or restarted writer may still use them.

options.text: Treat the uncertain remainder as abandoned and allocate a fresh non-overlapping range.
options.explanation: Correct. Never reissuing uncertain IDs avoids collisions, at the cost of namespace waste.

options.text: Restart its in-memory counter from the start of the old range.
options.explanation: That can reissue IDs already allocated before the crash.

options.text: Skip the coordinator and pick any unused-looking range.
options.explanation: Another server may already own it; a local observation does not establish global ownership.

workedExample: A durable reservation records which values belong to the server. Once a crash makes its exact allocation position uncertain, preserve the reservation and waste the remainder. Larger ranges reduce coordination frequency but can waste more values.

prompt: A usability review flags that your counter-based codes are sequential: `aZ3kQ9x` is followed by `aZ3kQ9y`, revealing sequential allocation. Private-link access control is handled separately. Which algebraic approach keeps codes collision-free and 7 characters long?

options.text: Switch to random 7-character codes and retry on collision.
options.explanation: This can produce unique stored codes with atomic code collision detection and retries, but it is a different allocation method rather than the requested algebraic rearrangement of counters.
Wrong. Snowflake IDs are also time-ordered and largely predictable (timestamp plus machine plus sequence), and they can require 11 base62 characters, breaking the 7-character requirement.

options.text: Apply a bijective permutation to the counter (e.g. multiply by a constant sharing no factor with the code-space size and keep the remainder, understanding that this is only obfuscation) before base62-encoding.
options.explanation: Correct. A bijection (one-to-one mapping) over all 3.5 trillion 7-character values maps each counter value to a unique code, so it stays collision-free, and it can obscure the raw sequence, but a simple multiplier leaves a recoverable pattern. This guarantees uniqueness, not secrecy: at 10% occupancy random probes hit valid links about 10% of the time.

options.text: Rate limit the redirect endpoint so enumeration takes longer.
options.explanation: Rate limiting can reduce probing opportunities, but it does not rearrange sequential codes or establish their uniqueness. Its effectiveness depends on the enforced scope and attacker resources.

workedExample: A bijection rearranges a finite set one-to-one: every input still has exactly one distinct output in the same code space. Multiplication followed by remainder has that property when the multiplier and space size are coprime. It hides the raw sequence from casual inspection but leaves recoverable patterns; it is not encryption or authorisation. Keep private-link access controls separate and never reuse or wrap allocated counters.
